stories.headline: Update: Trump Says U.S.-Iran Deal to Be Signed 'Shortly' as Strait of Hormuz Tensions Persist
stories.summary:
President Trump announced at a news conference in Evian-les-Bains, France, that a deal with Iran would be signed "shortly" — potentially as soon as Thursday. The agreement, described by Vice President Vance as "about a page and a half" and "very general," contains 14 points including an end to fighting, a commitment that Iran will never acquire a nuclear weapon, and a $300 billion redevelopment package for Iran. Both sides agreed to hold further talks on a final agreement within 60 days; the fate of Iran's nuclear program remains to be negotiated in those subsequent talks.

The announcement comes as Iran seized two cargo ships in the Strait of Hormuz, a move that followed Trump's declaration of a U.S. blockade of the waterway. Iranian negotiators have said Tehran "will decide the right of passage" through the strait, and the waterway remains largely closed as ships wait in the Gulf. Energy markets have experienced sharp swings since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

Trump also said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu needed "to be more responsible with respect to Lebanon," a signal of U.S.-Israeli friction. Many Lebanese remain skeptical that the broader agreement will end fighting between Israel and Hezbollah. An earlier Israeli strike on Beirut had threatened to derail the deal before it reached its current stage.

For Iranians, the central question is whether the deal will reduce prices and the fear of renewed war rather than who claimed victory. Hard-liners in Tehran have pushed back against the agreement, and the Iranian government faces the challenge of selling its terms to a divided domestic audience. The conflict has already raised global energy costs, with gas prices in the U.S. running roughly 79 cents higher per gallon than a year ago.

stories.headline: Trump's Economic Approval Rating Falls to Record Low in New Poll
stories.summary:
A new PBS NewsHour/NPR/Marist poll finds that only 33 percent of Americans approve of President Trump's handling of the economy, the lowest figure recorded since Marist began asking the question in 2019. Sixty percent of Americans overall disapprove. The result is also lower than the lowest economic approval rating recorded for former President Biden during his term.

The slide is being driven in part by persistent pain at the gas pump and rising food costs. Gas prices remain about 79 cents per gallon higher than a year ago, and 78 percent of Americans said gas prices have affected their household budgets. Notably, 54 percent of white voters without a college degree — a group Trump won decisively in 2024 — now disapprove of his economic handling.

Trump's supporters, however, largely remain with him: 77 percent of those who voted for him in 2024 still approve of his economic stewardship. Analysts note that some supporters who blamed high prices on Biden may now attribute them to corporate price gouging rather than to Trump's policies, partially cushioning his numbers within his base.

Trump's economic credibility was a central pillar of his 2024 campaign. The erosion of that advantage — particularly among working-class voters — marks a significant shift heading toward the 2026 midterms. Gas prices have dropped about 50 cents per gallon from their recent peak, but analysts say many consumers have not yet registered that relief.

stories.headline: Trump Poised to Roll Out New Tariffs as Treasury Refunds Nearly $22 Billion in Unlawful Duties
stories.summary:
The U.S. Treasury disbursed nearly $22 billion in reimbursements to importers in May alone for tariffs courts have ruled were unlawfully collected, meaning tariff revenue is currently flowing out of government coffers faster than it is coming in. The administration is simultaneously preparing to introduce a new round of tariffs, according to Bloomberg, raising questions about the coherence of trade policy at a moment of acute economic sensitivity.

Critics argue the original tariff structure was an "inexplicable mix" that failed to achieve the stated goal of leveraging reciprocal market openings from trading partners. Supporters of the approach have argued that strategic tariffs can paradoxically expand economic freedom by forcing negotiations, though that outcome has not materialized in practice according to analysts cited in the reporting.

The developments add complexity to Trump's economic standing. His administration has repeatedly pointed to tariffs as a tool for rebuilding American manufacturing and extracting concessions from rivals, but the combination of court-ordered refunds and new levies signals ongoing legal and political turbulence around the policy. U.S. trading partners are closely watching what new tariff actions take shape.

The tariff situation intersects with the broader inflation picture that is already weighing on Trump's approval ratings. Higher import costs have contributed to elevated prices for consumer goods, and any fresh round of tariffs could add further upward pressure at a politically difficult moment for the administration.

stories.headline: Gunfire and Explosions Reported at Airport in Niger's Capital Niamey
stories.summary:
Residents of Niamey told the BBC that gunfire and explosions erupted early Thursday morning at the entrance of Diori Hamani International Airport in Niger's capital, with the exchange lasting approximately two hours beginning around 6 a.m. local time. Niger's army is reported to have repelled the attack and is now hunting fleeing assailants who allegedly abandoned their weapons at the scene. Authorities had not officially commented as of initial reports.

The attack follows a near-identical assault on the same airport in January, which an affiliate of the Islamic State claimed responsibility for. In that incident, four military personnel were injured and 20 attackers were killed. Niger's military government, in power for three years, thanked Russia for assistance in foiling the January attack and accused leaders of France, Benin, and Ivory Coast of backing the assailants — accusations for which no evidence was provided.

Niger has been battling a jihadist insurgency for a decade and, alongside neighbors Burkina Faso and Mali, is governed by a military junta that came to power partly on the failure of civilian governments to contain the violence. In recent weeks, Niamey authorities demolished neighborhoods near the airport citing terrorist risks and expanded the perimeter fence and surveillance infrastructure around the facility.

The recurrence of attacks on the same strategic site underscores the fragility of security in the Sahel region and the limits of both military governance and Russian security assistance in containing Islamist militancy across West Africa.
